episodes.200679: A thunderstorm produced a waterspout over Lake Griffin near Silver Lake.
episodes.200706: A deep stream of moisture was pulled northwestward from the Atlantic Ocean into the mountains of south-central Pennsylvania around an upper level low centered over the Ohio Valley during the afternoon and evening hours of May 13. 2025. This led to extensive flooding and flash flooding across Somerset County and southwestern Bedford County, and more sporadic flooding from the remainder of Bedford County eastward into Fulton and Franklin counties.
episodes.200860: A slow moving closed upper level low originating from the Gulf of America brought anomalous moisture into the area. A long duration period of rain ensued, with rain rates exceeding two inches an hour during the afternoon of May 13th. The slow moving storms coupled with training led to localized rainfall totals of four to eight inches across western Maryland, with lesser amounts of two to four inches across central Maryland. Most of this rain fell in a 6 hour period, resulting in flash flooding especially across western Maryland.
episodes.200862: A slow moving closed upper level low originating from the Gulf of America brought anomalous moisture into the area. A long duration period of rain ensued, with rain rates exceeding two inches an hour during the afternoon of May 13th. The slow moving storms coupled with training led to localized rainfall totals of four to eight inches across Mineral County, WV, with lesser amounts of two to four inches across the rest of the eastern panhandle. Most of this rain fell in a 6 hour period, resulting in flash flooding especially across Mineral County.
episodes.200884: A slow moving closed upper level low originating from the Gulf of America brought anomalous moisture into the area. A long duration period of rain ensued, with rain rates exceeding two inches an hour during the afternoon and evening of May 13th. The slow moving storms coupled with training led to localized rainfall totals of four to eight inches across the Blue Ridge, with lesser amounts of two to four inches along and west of I-95. Flooding lingered into the morning hours of May 14th.
episodes.201278: Thunderstorms brought strong to severe wind gusts to the area during the evening of May 12th. The highest wind gust was 62 mph at the Poplar RAWS station in Roosevelt county.
episodes.201309: A surface trough extending along the I-74 corridor triggered widely scattered showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon of May 13th.  Given enhanced low-level vorticity in the vicinity of the boundary, a couple of the cells produced brief landspout tornadoes as they first developed and before precipitation began to fall.  Three tornadoes were reported...including an EF-U near Emden in Logan County, and EF-U just north of Champaign in Champaign County, and an EF-0 that caused minor tree damage southwest of Toulon in Stark County.
episodes.201348: A mid-level trough over the Tennessee valley region produced two main waves of showers and storms across eastern sections of central North Carolina. The first wave came through in the early morning hours, which produced two tornadoes in Edgecombe County. A second wave of storms developed in the afternoon and evening, producing isolated wind damage across the region.
episodes.201409: Active weather in the form of flash flooding and strong thunderstorms prevailed over southeast Ohio on May 13th as a result of a nearby frontal boundary. The original front stalled across the Ohio Valley on the 11th, then dissolved over the area while a disturbance slowly approached from the southwest for the next several days. This set the stage for heavy downpours and strong thunderstorms amid the hot and humid airmass planted overhead.||During the afternoon and evening of May 13th, strong thunderstorms downed trees and power lines across portions of the area. Heavy rainfall within these storms also led to widespread half to one and a half in rainfall amounts, with a localized spots of 2 to 3 inch amounts within southeast Ohio. Heavy rain over previously saturated ground prompted flash flooding in Athens, Jackson, Meigs, and Perry Counties. This impacted not only local roadways, but also the first floors of several homes in Perry County along with a nearby church. The threat for severe weather and flash flooding came to an end on May 14th once a break in the weather pattern took shape with the help of building high pressure.
episodes.201410: A frontal boundary stalled over the state of West Virginia beginning on May 11th, then dissolved over the area while a disturbance approached from the southwest on the 12th. Widespread precipitation progressed northward across the area on the 12th, followed by rounds of scattered showers and thunderstorms continuing to impact the area over the next couple of days as an upper level trough and surface low pressure system traversed the Ohio Valley. ||During the afternoon and evening of May 13th, strong thunderstorms downed trees and power lines across portions of the area. Heavy rainfall within storms also led to widespread half to one and a half in rainfall amounts, with pockets of 2 to 4 inch rainfall amounts across portions of West Virginia. Heavy rain over previously saturated ground prompted flash flooding in Braxton, Clay, Harrison, Jackson, and Lewis Counties. Mudslides also occurred in Boone and Lewis Counties, with one instance of a mobile home being evacuated due to water reaching chest level.||The risk for severe weather concluded by May 14th once the surface low sprinted off the eastern seaboard. Floodwaters also receded in the wake of showers and storms.
episodes.201511: Slow moving thunderstorms produced isolated areas of flash flooding.
episodes.201513: A thunderstorm produced a severe wind gust near Wrightsville Beach.
episodes.201578: A couple storms formed during the late night into early morning hours. One storm became severe and produced wind damage in Jones County.
episodes.201605: A weak warm front and surface trough lifted north across the coastal waters of Eastern North Carolina. As this occurred, scattered showers and isolated thunderstorms developed and lifted north along the aforementioned warm front with a few of these storms becoming strong to severe in nature. The strongest storms brought damaging wind gusts to portions of the coastal waters near Cape Lookout and along the Coastal waters near Nags Head NC.
episodes.202150: A board low pressure system facilitated unsettled conditions across the region with cold air aloft supporting weak afternoon instability. During the afternoon hours of May 12th a cold air funnel cloud was reported in shower activity near Eugene, Oregon.
episodes.202395: An upper low positioned over the Tennessee Valley, with numerous shortwaves rotating through it, brought several rounds of showers and thunderstorms to the area for a few days. Surface low pressure over the Midwest also helped to prompt the development of thunderstorms. A plume of moisture pushed northward into the area from the Carolinas, and helped convective initiation, despite some dry air also in the area. SBCAPE rose to between 1000-1500 J/kg, with moderate bulk shear of 25 to 30 knots, led to some storms becoming severe, and produce several instances of hail.
episodes.202466: In the midst of hot and humid weather, eastern Kentucky experienced several days of strong thunderstorms from May 13th through the 16th. As daytime heating got underway during the late morning hours, shower and thunderstorm development thrived in this unstable environment, with some storms growing strong enough to produce damaging wind gusts. This resulted in downed trees and power lines in the area, causing local power outages for many residents in eastern Kentucky. The weather pattern finally changed on the evening of May 16th after a cold front swept through the Ohio Valley and Central Appalachians.
episodes.202625: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced strong winds in excess of 34 knots across the area.  In addition, a fair weather waterspout was observed.
episodes.202805: An area of low pressure formed across a warm front along the Virginia/North Carolina border on May 13. Scattered storms formed across the Piedmont during the late afternoon and evening in a moist air mass. A few storms were severe and produced damaging winds.
episodes.202806: An area of low pressure formed across a warm front along the Virginia/North Carolina border on May 13. Scattered storms formed across the Piedmont during the late afternoon and evening in a moist air mass. These storms produced locally heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding.
episodes.202807: An area of low pressure formed across a warm front along the Virginia/North Carolina border on May 13. This allowed for a period of elevated east-southeast winds across the Chesapeake Bay, Lower James River, and North Carolina coastal waters. These winds were enhanced by convection moving across the water.
episodes.203085: A slow-moving thunderstorm during the evening of May 13th produced between 2 and 3.5 inches of rain in western Muskingum County, resulting in flash flooding.
episodes.203368: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed across upstate South Carolina during the evening. One storm produced a brief tornado in Abbeville County. Storms and clusters tended to move slowly, resulting in locally heavy rainfall, with isolated flash flooding developing where multiple storms moved over the same areas.
episodes.203404: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the Piedmont during the early afternoon. One of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Cabarrus County.
episodes.203574: A surface front associated with an area of low pressure moving across the southern United States slowly approached Florida from the eastern Gulf. The moist air mass ahead of the front allowed for flooding from excessive rainfall and for strong to severe thunderstorms to develop.
episodes.207240: With high pressure exiting to the east of the state, a weak low pressure system started to form to our southwest, slowly moving northeast, making it through western KY between 18 and 21Z. This was accompanied by a closed upper level low, which was allowing for strong advection of warm and especially moist air into the region, focused across the east part of Kentucky. The result was showers and thunderstorms that produced heavy rain in some areas, including Estill and Letcher counties, which saw some isolated flooding.

Photographs and video from social media, in addition to a special METAR from KEUG, indicate a funnel cloud developed around 1-2 miles northwest of the Eugene Airport.

Videos sent by public and local media show a waterspout developed over Lake Griffin in the Leesburg area near sunset. A confirmed report by the Leesburg fire department, |indicates the spout remained over water.
The Watauga River was observed flooded out of its banks across Dewitt Barnett Road.  No damage was reported to the road, which was reopened to traffic once the flooding receded.
Portions of Castleford Road were flooded and impassible due to flooding of a small creek running adjacent to the road. No damage was reported.

County comms reported flash flooding developed across the north side of the city of Greenwood after 3 to 5 inches of rain fell over the city in only 2-3 hours. The main impact was to Rocky Creek, which overflowed its banks and inundated portions of Haltiwanger Rd and Rockcreek Blvd. An apartment complex on Haltiwanger Rd was evacuated after bring threatened by floodwater. Multiple roads were reportedly closed throughout the city due to a combination of urban flash flooding and small stream inundation.

County comms reported flash flooding developed in the Laurens area and in Waterloo after a swath of 3 to 4 inches of rain fell in this area in 2-3 hours. Long Lick Branch overflowed its banks in the Waterloo area and inundated Todd Quarter Rd, which had to be closed. Harris Springs Rd was also inundated by water from Cane Creek. In the city of Laurens, the Little River overflowed its banks and flooded Little River Park. A tributary of the Little River flooded a portion of Fleming St, where a motorist became stranded in floodwater.

An EF-1 tornado developed just inside Edgecombe County north of the town of Fountain NC. The tornado traveled north, crossing route 258 and causing structural damage to a mobile home along with several snapped trees. It then entered a densely wooded, inaccessible area and it is unclear if the tornado remained on the ground continuously, but additional tree damage was found near the intersection of Otter Creek Church Rd and Wooten Rd. No additional damage was noted downwind of that intersection.

An EF-1 tornado formed on the south side of Pinetops. It then traveled northward through a baseball field, snapping several nearby trees and destroying the porch of a nearby house. The tornado continued northward across a field, resulting in additional structural and tree damage. The tornado skipped erratically to the northwest, eventually causing damage to trees and a house along Faith Baptist Church Rd, before dissipating in a field nearby.
